articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: Mine Entra embodies Second Republic’s consultative governance: President
more.description: Nqobile Bhebhe, nqobile.bhebhe@chronicle.co.zw PRESIDENT Mnangagwa has linked the Second Republic's consultative governance model to Zimbabwe's value-addition and beneficiation agenda, describing the Mine Entra Conference and Exhibition as a strategic platform where stakeholder engagement is shaping the country's mining and industrial future. In a speech read on his behalf by Vice-President Dr Constantino Chiwenga at the official opening of the 29th Mine Entra Conference and Exhibition in Bulawayo on Friday, President Mnangagwa said Government was intensifying a whole-of-government-and-society approach to accelerate the attainment of Vision 2030. The President said the approach was reinforced during last week's Zanu-PF Politburo meeting, where emphasis was placed on broad-based consultation and grassroots participation in national development. https://youtu.be/5LKnWAfIoMQ Last week, ZANU-PF held its monthly Politburo session. At that meeting, I highlighted that under this current phase of the Second Republic, my administration is scaling up the whole-of-government-and-society approach. Though increased stakeholder engagement and grassroots participation, we are strengthening participatory democracy and transitioning our governance style to be based on consultation and practical problem-solving, he said. President Mnangagwa said the people remained at the centre of Government's development agenda as Zimbabwe pushes towards becoming an upper middle-income economy by 2030. The people-centered ZANPF government is determined to accelerate the realization of Vision 2030 and the development that imparts the generality of our pipo. He said the same philosophy of consultation and collaboration underpinned Mine Entra, which has evolved beyond a traditional mining exhibition into a strategic forum for advancing the country's mining value chains and industrial transformation. It is in this spirit that I am honoured to be back in Bulawayo to officiate at this year's 20th edition of the Mining, Engineering, and Transport Conference. Undoubtedly, this event has grown in impact with far-reaching influence on the ongoing transformation of the mining sector and the overall socio-economic development of our beloved motherland, Zimbabwe. It has transitioned from being a trade show to become a platform where ideas are crystallised, partnerships forged, and policy meets practice. The President said the transformation being pursued through Mine Entra is consistent with the Second Republic's vision of building a modern, value-added mining industry that retains greater value from the country's vast mineral wealth. Under the Second Republic, the aim is to build a value-added mining economy. Through beneficiation and industrialisation, we want to guarantee maximum value for the board-given natural resources. Ultimately, the mining industry must not only aid in expanding the national wealth or economic growth, but result in tangible benefits to the ordinary citizens. President Mnangagwa noted that despite Zimbabwe's abundant mineral endowment, the country had for many years exported raw minerals while domestic industries lagged behind. Zimbabwe is acclaimed for high deposits of critical minerals and for a long time was a renowned source of raw minerals for other global industries while our own became stagnant and antiquated. We have said not anymore under my leadership and administration. That narrative is changing. I urge stakeholders and partners to decisively and boldly transition to this new reality. The steps we are taking have not been undertaken by many on our continent. He expressed confidence that Zimbabwe has the capacity and determination to successfully implement the ambitious transformation agenda. I am confident that we are up to the challenge. The President's remarks underscore Government's view that national development is best driven through continuous engagement between policymakers, industry, investors, academia and communities, with Mine Entra serving as one of the key platforms where such collaboration translates into practical outcomes. The annual exhibition has increasingly become a meeting point for Government, mining companies, equipment manufacturers, financial institutions and technology providers to deliberate on policies, unlock investment opportunities and strengthen value addition and beneficiation across the mining sector. The linkage between the resolutions of the Zanu-PF Politburo and the objectives of Mine Entra reflects the Second Republic's governance model, which places premium on consultation, stakeholder participation and evidence-based policy implementation while accelerating industrialisation through mineral beneficiation.

more.title: More than 500 mourners gather in UK to remember Nothabo Tshuma and daughters
more.description: A remembrance service has been held for a mother and her two children believed to have been murdered in their home. Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, 42, and her daughters Natalie, 15, and Nala, five, were found dead in Great Denham, near Bedford, on 6 July, and an inquest which opened into their deaths on Tuesday said they died from head injuries. [caption id=attachment_5426857 align=alignnone width=1600] More than 500 mourners gather in UK to remember Nothabo Tshuma and daughters (pix courtesy of Zimbo live news)[/caption] Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, 45, arrested in Johannesburg on suspicion of murdering his wife and two children, remains in custody in South Africa. Almost 500 mourners attended the service at Bedford's Corn Exchange, with tributes read out including one from Nala's class teacher, Nikki Woodworth, who said, her hugs were legendary. Michelle Ncube, Zandile's cousin, told those gathered: Words cannot begin to describe the depth of our loss. We grieve the loss of the future that have been stolen from them and from us. She blessed us with her dry wit, her intelligence. She loved gardening. But she didn't just nurture flowers, she nurtured people. She said Zandile was completely devoted to her daughters and that everything she did was with their future in mind. [caption id=attachment_5426862 align=alignnone width=1600] More than 500 mourners gather in UK to remember Nothabo Tshuma and daughters (pix courtesy of Zimbo live news)[/caption] Zandile's sister, who lives in Zimbabwe, sent a message which was read out by an aunt. She was more than my sister...sharing a bond through a lifetime of memories, she wrote. [The loss has] created a void in our hearts and our family that words can hardly describe...life will never be the same without them. Gemma Gibson, headmistress of Bedford Girls School, where Natalie attended, was also at the service. When we think of Natalie as a young girl, we picture her smile first...it simply reflected the beautiful person she was, she said. She was a composed and thoughtful pupil who loved learning...but it was her kindness that left the biggest impression. Natalie represented the school 107 times at lacrosse, tennis and hockey among other sports. She will forever be loved and remembered by all of us at Bedford Girls' School, the head teacher said. The organiser of the service, Jabu Ncube, had known Zandile for 20 years, meeting her at university. He asked the gathering: How do you find words to confirm something that is unspeakable? How do you find words to comprehend something that is incomprehensible? I have the task of finding the words. Remember them as the angels that they are. Toby was one of several of Zandile's colleagues who worked with her at Forensic Risk Alliance in the forensic data analytics team in London. He told those who gathered that she showed exceptional professionalism...sharp intelligence and a passion for her work with kindness. Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma was arrested on an unlicensed firearms charge in Johannesburg on 10 July, and later appeared in court accused of illegally possessing firearms. South African courts will decide whether a British extradition request meets the legal requirements for his transfer back to the UK. Statements from the coroner's officers revealed the mother died from head injuries while the children's cause of death was listed as blunt force head injuries. The inquest was adjourned to a date to be determined. Funerals for all three members of the family are to take place next week in Zimbabwe. - BBC
